utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Good afternoon to everyone. May we take the appearances for today, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good afternoon Your Honours, Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Slobodan Zecevic, Slobodan Cvijetic, Eugene O'Sullivan and Ms. Tatjana Savic appearing for Stanisic Defence this afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. For Stojan Zupljanin, it's Aleksandar Aleksic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We have been alerted by the Court Officer that there are a number of housekeeping matters which Mr. Zecevic wishes to raise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, thank you very much. Your Honours, the Defence of Stanisic appreciates the position of the Trial Chamber where the Trial Chamber is involved in a number of cases at the moment. However, I must raise our grave concern on the following situation. There is seven pending motions filed by the Stanisic Defence. Now, two of the motions deal with our request to admit evidence based on Rule 92 quater. Three motions are motions to amend our 65 ter list. There is one motion for binding order to government of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina dated 19th of May. And there is a motion to admit documents and selected footnote documents from our Expert Bajagic report. Now, Your Honours, this is our penultimate witness. We have one more witness to go, and before all seven of these motions are decided upon, we will not be able to file our bar table motion. Now, that will of course make our position on the closing of our case very -- will keep it somewhere in vein, you see, because the moment when we file our bar table motion, then we will be in a position, perhaps, to rest our case. The second thing -- the second thing, Your Honours, our last witness would be our last opportunity before the bar table motion to introduce some important evidence. Now, this situation will actually impair our ability to present important evidence to the Trial Chamber. Because in case Your Honours would not accept our motions as stated, we would -- we could use the opportunity to lead the evidence with the last witness on a number of these documents. Now, I can do that in any case but then it will just prolong the time and it might be the fact that Your Honours will admit these documents based on our motions, so then I would be repeating and using the court time and resources. Now, this is a very grave concern that we are having concerning this issue, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If I might interrupt briefly, Mr. Zecevic, how many of the outstanding motions are awaiting responses from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can assist with that. I'm not aware of three motions to add to the 65 ter list. I am aware of one which was served, I was going to say, filed on the 3rd of June and we are going to respond. We've got to Friday and we are going to respond to it. One which was produced yesterday which appears to relate to documents which the Defence wish to show this witness. There was a great deal of confusion about that. And so in respect of that, we are really waiting to see how the Defence deal with these documents with the witness. I mean, that's what they say in the motion and it may well be we don't feel the necessity to respond. But certainly we will be responding to the one of 3rd of June. And one on the 6th of May, I must admit I have absolutely no recollection whether we responded or decide we were not going to respond. Mr. Smith, helpfully, thinks we did respond already. Clearly we must have, it's the 6th of May and we were going to respond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I can summarise, Your Honours, it appears that there are two motions that the Office of the Prosecutor needs to responds to, or depends if they want, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm told we did respond to the 6th of May motion on the 18th of May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. The -- we will consider the implications of these motions as Mr. Zecevic has articulated the affect of any -- not merely any delay, but the affect of the progress of the resolution of these outstanding matters, and we fully appreciate how an early answer is required. It's something that we would have to give consideration to, of course, as judges outside of court.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's just two other matters which really arise out of that. The first is: The Defence filed a response to our application to have documents put to Mr. Bjelosevic de-MFI'd. I mean, it's not the right expression, but we are going to be seeking leave to respond to a response because we say it contains some inaccuracies, and we are hoping to file that application for leave to respond to their response tomorrow, just so that Your Honours know. But the second matter is this, of course: We are obviously moving fairly speedily into Mr. Zupljanin's Defence case, and I appreciate this has not been mentioned by Mr. Aleksic, but he has made an application for a number of witnesses to be called under the Rule 92 bis, which we've objected to. And, clearly, I think from all sides, we'd like to know about that too and Mr. Zecevic in particular, I imagine. Not Mr. Zecevic, sorry, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only add that my learned friend Mr. Krgovic spoke about this last week and we await the decision of the Trial Chamber on this after they rule on our submission based on Rule 92 ter. We have one witness based on Rule 92 quater and then we'll decide whether we will call all these witnesses. I can't give you an opinion on this right now until we've had the ruling of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. One other matter. Mr. Zecevic, we have seen your e-mail communication about the two witnesses whom you no longer intend to call and may we have that confirmed for the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. I advised -- as promised, I advised yesterday morning the Trial Chamber and the other party -- I mean, all the parties to this trial that the Stanisic Defence will not be calling witnesses Nikola Milanovic and witness Branko Vlac [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, the last thing was I don't know whether Your Honours reached a decision on Mr. Krgovic's application that there should be a week's break between the end of the Stanisic's case and the beginning of his case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The short answer is no, but the -- that is in a sense tied up with the matters which Mr. Zecevic raised, so it is unfortunate that we can't give a more clearer or more tidy indication as to what is going to happen, but by -- certainly by next week, we must, for the sake of efficiency, have sorted out these matters. Thanks

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I am reminded by my brother Judge Delvoie that when I said the short answer is no, what I meant is that we hadn't made a decision, so unless the parties --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understood that. I didn't read into it that there's not going to be a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So, Mr. Zecevic, could you call your next witness, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Our next witness is MS-003, Mr. Simo Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir, and welcome to the Tribunal and thank you for coming to The Hague to give your testimony. May I first of all ask you if you can hear me in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could I then please ask you to read the solemn declaration which is being put to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very well, sir. You may be seated. Could you please state your name and your date and place of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Simo Tusevljak. I was born on the 12th of February, 1965, in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tusevljak, have you ever testified before this Court?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I have, as a Defence witness in the case against General Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. And by the way, have you testified in other domestic courts in your country of residence about the matters relating to the war in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I have never testified at home on these issues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Very well. Since you have been here as a witness and have given some testimony already, you are familiar with the proceedings that apply to this Court, but maybe I should just resume for the matter of clarity that you are being called as a witness by the Defence for Mr. Stanisic, and Mr. Stanisic's counsel has asked for six hours to examine you in chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: I apologise, 12 hours to examine you in chief. And Mr. Krgovic --

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will say an hour just as a matter of precaution but I don't really expect to have any questions for this witness. Out of caution, I will say an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And this was the Defence counsel for Mr. Zupljanin speaking. So counsel for Mr. Stanisic has asked for 12 hours; counsel for Mr. Zupljanin, possibly one hour; and counsel for the Prosecution in cross-examination has asked for?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've met Mr. Tusevljak before. If Mr. Tusevljak can be persuaded to keep his answers short, I would hope that 10 hours would suffice. But as a matter of caution, as I say, having met Mr. Tusevljak, 12 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Korner. So there we have it. This means that you will certainly be kept to testify for all of this week and possibly most of next week also. You also know already, Mr. Tusevljak, that we run the sessions in 90 minutes, after which we have to change the tapes and while we change the tapes, we normally take 20 minutes break. I should also advise you to make sure that you do not respond too quickly to the questions put to you because we have interpreters who interpret what you say into English and French. And if counsel and the witness are overlapping, it is impossible for the interpreters to catch what you are saying, in which case nothing comes out of it. So in your own interest and certainly in the interests of the Judges, we kindly ask you to follow the cursor on the screen, I think to your left, where you will see that it moves. So as long as text is still rolling on the monitor, please withhold your answer and do not answer before you see the cursor has stopped. So as I said, please observe to hold a small pause between question and answer, and, also, as Ms. Korner has suggested, do keep your answers short and to the point, listen carefully to what is being asked and try to respond to the question as shortly as you can. And finally, Mr. Tusevljak, I need to remind you that the solemn declaration that you have just made to us does oblige you to tell the truth and nothing but truth and the whole truth, and if you don't do that, you risk to be prosecuted for perjury, and I should remind you that there is a severe penalty for providing false or incomplete information to the Chamber. With these words, I give the floor to Mr. Zecevic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. If the usher could assist me, this is a binder for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Tusevljak.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, when you were born -- please tell us where you were born?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I was born in Sarajevo, in Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Have you completed university education?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I completed the police academy in Skopje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I would like to ask you to be slow in your answers because first my question has it to be interpreted into English and then your reply needs to be interpreted as well. Tell me, it says here that you completed the police academy in Skopje, can you explain to me what kind of university that is that you completed in Skopje and what year that was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I enrolled in 1984 and completed the university of security in 1988 [Realtime transcript read in error "1998"] in Skopje. That was the only university of the interior in the former Yugoslavia. Apart from studying the law, we also studied police affairs, criminology, forensics, methodology, the operative and everything else that the police deals with and that the organs of the interior deal with. That's where I learned my expertise at that university. And after completing my studies, I started working at the SJB in Novi Grad, Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What year did you start working in the Novi Grad police station in Sarajevo, and at what position?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I started working in 1989 on the 1st of March as crime prevention inspector. We dealt with regular crimes, theft, and we also dealt with serious crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, it was recorded on page 9, line 22, that you completed the university in 1998. What year did you complete the university in Skopje?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tusevljak, until when did you work in the Novi Grad SJB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I worked in the Novi Grad SJB until the 1st of September, 1990, and then I became an inspector in the SUP in Sarajevo. I was a co-ordinator.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't catch the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, could you repeat the last part of your answer, which was missed by the interpreters. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I worked as an inspector in the Sarajevo SUP on property theft and I was co-ordinator for property theft for all of the city of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what was the relationship between the town SUP and the SJB, the Novi Grad SJB, I mean in terms of hierarchy, in terms of the hierarchy that was valid in the structure of the MUP of the then Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The town SUP existed only in Sarajevo, and there were ten Sarajevo municipalities which were a part of it. We were above the Novi Grad SJB. However, since there was also a CSB in Sarajevo which was -- which also contained all the police stations in Sarajevo, the role was that of a co-ordination role and a monitoring the situation of crime in these ten Sarajevo municipalities. Apart from this, the town SUP contained departments, forensic departments which the SJBs didn't have, so the town SUP provided services, forensic services to all the SJBs in the city of Sarajevo in relation to general crimes. There was also fire prevention department, there were inspectors, there was a department that dealt with foreigners, and there was a department for white-collar crime which the SJBs also didn't have. It was the town SUP was the only one that had this. And they dealt with minor crimes. The CSB had a similar department that dealt with more serious crimes of that type.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, the town SUP of Sarajevo, as for this co-ordination role that it had, with regard to the crime prevention police, did they have this kind of co-ordination role in view of the other segments that existed in these ten public security stations in the territory of the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, for the most part, this was a role of co-ordination, although there were services there. There was the chief of police for the town of Sarajevo, that's for the uniform police, and they had their own departments and then there was the police station for traffic safety within the town police station. I worked there only for three years. I don't really know all of that, but basically my work focused on crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you came to the town SUP of Sarajevo, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: My immediate superior, or rather, the chief of the general crime department was Goran Macar. The head of sector was Idriz Hodzic, and very soon after that he was replaced by Jozo Leotar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat Mr. Leotar's first name?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Jozo Leotar.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Tusevljak, in the summer of 1991 was a group established at the level of the town SUP of Sarajevo, and if so, what did they do and what was your role within that context?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: As co-ordinator in terms of property-related crime, in the town SUP we received information about all crimes committed in the territory of the town of Sarajevo. Our role was to follow the crime situation, and when we would notice certain trends or a large number of unresolved cases from a particular field, then we established operative groups consisting of operatives from public security stations and then these groups resolved those crimes. Throughout 1991, there was a major escalation in the commission of crime in the territory of the town of Sarajevo, and on certain days even up to 500 crimes would be committed by unknown perpetrators. For the most part, this was break and entry related to apartments, cars, department stores, kiosks, theft of vehicles. And in the general crime department in the town SUP, our assessment was that operative groups that can operate in the territory of the entire town would be far more efficient in combatting groups of criminals. Already in the summer of 1991 from all public security stations that were in the territory of the town provided their best policemen or inspectors and we set out, all of this with a view to solving as many cases as possible and to make it possible for citizens to live the most normal life possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, just tell us something, you mentioned this general crime service, as you call it. What does that mean actually? What crimes do they work on, or at least did they work on in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The general crime service dealt with investigating and documenting crimes of a classical nature, as it were. That is to say, robbery, aggravated robbery; at any rate, crimes that belonged to the field of property-related crime. At this point -- at this point, I would like to clarify something. Public security stations that were within the town SUP worked only on resolving crimes that were dealt with by basic courts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say basic courts and their jurisdiction, does that mean that public security stations dealt with less serious crimes, if I can put it that way, or not?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. That's what it means. Public security stations dealt with crimes that were less serious, although if a more serious crime were committed in the territory of a particular police station, then members of the crime police of that station provided all possible assistance to the members of the centre for public security services of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean, Mr. Tusevljak, in order to clarify the matter, if a more serious crime is committed, the investigation of that particular crime would fall under the CSB, the Security Services Centre; is that right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, since that serious crime was committed in that particular territory, then members of the public security station would provide all a possible support, logistical support, and any other support to the members of the CSB who were in charge of these more serious crimes; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tusevljak, in your view, what was the key problem in 1991 in terms of so many crimes not being solved?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I think that the basic problem was the fact that in 1992 there was already a disruption --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, I asked you about 1991.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In 1991, there were already certain upheavals in the territory of the former Yugoslavia. The war in Croatia was well underway, and in the Ministry of the Interior, the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also in the CSB Sarajevo there were more and more people who did not really have anything to do with police work up until then. There were more and more people coming in who were employed in the police, but were not involved in police work at all, or were totally unfamiliar with the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was that one of the reasons why this group was established, the one that you co-ordinated at the level of the town SUP of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: One of the main reasons was our wish to show all public security stations that they could work on solving crimes. And through this operative group, we tried to force them, as well, to work more in their respective areas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of results were achieved by this operative group of yours during the course of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I think we had excellent results, above average at that, because I remember that it was only in November 1991 that we had 100 cases that involved detention.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say cases that involved detention, what do you mean? Do you mean that the perpetrators of the crime involved had been apprehended and that they were remanded in custody?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. We discovered the perpetrators and we filed a report with the prosecutor's office and we handed him over.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, you mentioned a number of policemen who were from elsewhere, who were not from Sarajevo and who were not familiar with Sarajevo, where did most of these policemen come from, to the best of your knowledge or in your view?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, 90 per cent of these persons came from the territory of Sandzak in Serbia, or the north of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since I'm not sure that the Trial Chamber is familiar with this, as well as the rest, tell me, the territory of Sandzak is partly in Serbia and partly in Montenegro; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the predominant ethnicity in Sandzak?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Muslim. Bosniak nowadays, they've changed their name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: These persons that you spoke about that were employed in the police force and were not familiar with the town of Sarajevo, were they ethnic Muslims, or rather, ethnic Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: One hundred per cent Bosniak ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, sir, in your opinion, did politics and policymakers interfere in the work of the Ministry of the Interior in Bosnia in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, I can speak about that from the point of view of a policeman who literally worked in the street at the time. Our problems were manifested in the following: When it was evident that certain persons had committed a crime, and if we established that during the course of our own work, we could not prosecute them further. Unfortunately, these were ordinary criminals, but it was the very first time that that kind of thing happened then. If a person had any kind of ties to a political party, a national one, if we were to bring that person before the public prosecutor, very often we were not allowed to take the measures that we had requested, measures that had been standard procedure up until then.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what measures do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, custody, searching apartments, qualifying the crime involved and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, Mr. Tusevljak, do you have any knowledge regarding illegal arming in 1991 or the latter part of 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Once again, I can speak of two particular cases from my very own experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The first question was when the traffic police stopped a vehicle which was a minivan owned by the Islamic religious community in Sarajevo. In that vehicle they found 400 sniper rifles which were travelling -- which were being transported from the Zrak factory in Sarajevo which was the factory producing optical material, and they were allegedly headed to the hunting association in Citluk. Since we had an ability to monitor radio communications of our police on the ground in the field, we knew right away about this. We requested that this vehicle be set aside and taken to the special unit base where we wanted to check their documents. However, by the time we reached that base, the vehicle had already been released; that is to say, it had been allowed to continue moving. This had been approved by somebody from the top echelons of the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina; whereas we were not allowed to do our work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, tell me, was it customary for weapons to be transported in this way; that is to say, in a minivan owned by the Islamic religious community?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Absolutely not. It was not possible for somebody to transport 400 sniper rifles allegedly intended for the hunting association.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell us about this second case?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, the second case was about the police stopping a truck, trailer truck, or rather, two trailer trucks, transporting weapons and military equipment. And this happened in Hadzici. By the time the policemen of the town SUP had reached the area, one of the trailer trucks had managed to flee the location; whereas the other one, pursuant to the order of the chief of that police station, had been released because allegedly its papers were in order. I would like to tell you that the standard procedure up to 1991, as well as today, was such that all transport of weapons and ammunition had to have a proper police permit. And the police was duty-bound in such cases to escort the vehicles with this kind of goods via its territory, precisely to prevent any possible abuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In both of these cases that you described to us, was this procedure followed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, because had it been followed, we wouldn't have reacted because we would have had the decision of the relevant body, the body in charge of these matters. In Bosnia-Herzegovina, this is referred as so-called B materiel. The police escorted on a daily basis transport carrying explosives or weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Are you now referring to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I'm now referring to the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BH.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, was this procedure observed when, say, explosives were transported for the needs of some mines in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, all transport of explosives required that this procedure be observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Tusevljak, was this procedure observed also when hunting weapons were transported intended for the shops selling such goods to citizens?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I do not really study these matters in depth. However, in all cases involving large quantities of weapons, that is to say, not one rifle or five rifles, permits were needed and there needed to be police escort for such transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Tusevljak. Now, let us move to another topic. In the night before the 3rd and 4th of April in 1992 in Sarajevo, where were you and what was your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At that time I was -- I still occupied my position in the town SUP of Sarajevo performing the same type of work. However, at that point in time we received an order from the chief of sector Jozo Leotar that we had to have our own separate duty service. And this duty service of operatives was supposed to convey to us all information about the events taking place in the territory of the ten Sarajevo municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a question: What was the ethnicity of Mr. Jozo Leotar, your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: He was an ethnic Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what did you observe -- or, rather, were you on duty that night?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In addition to this duty service, we also had a mandatory task to tour, to patrol the town in our vehicles, as did the police stations in our -- under our jurisdiction, in our territory. This was already April, and as is well known, on the 30th of March a member of the Serbian wedding party was killed in Bascarsija. Barricades had already been erected around Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, but this murder took place on the 29th of February or the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm just trying to refresh the memory of the witness. I mean, this is not disputed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, it's not disputed, but if he wrongly links things, that may be relevant and he oughtn't be told when things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead, sir, and answer the question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Since it's been so many years and I'm still in the police business and I was involved in many events, as I still am today, I apologise for occasionally making a mistake when it comes to certain dates or days in the week. However, the killing of the member of the wedding party and the barricades is something that indeed took place in Sarajevo. Following these events, and once the law and order were seriously disturbed and various crimes committed, from murder to robberies and burglaries, the state of alert was raised in the town SUP and it required us to do this kind of work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it was my mistake since I pin-pointed the date. Please tell us what you saw that night when you were on duty service and patrolled the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: What we saw was that around all police stations there were armed civilians and that they literally controlled -- had the ability to prevent anyone from going in or coming out of the police station. They controlled access.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you inform your immediate superiors in the MUP about this?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Everything we observed on that night or any other night was conveyed to our immediate superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know who Enes Bezdrob and Ismet Dahic were?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Enes Bezdrob was chief of the Stari Grad SJB, whereas Ismet Dahic was the police commander in that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As you patrolled the town on that night, did you also go to the Stari Grad SJB to see Mr. Bezdrob and Mr. Dahic? And what did you find there, if so?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: When I -- the night when I went to the Stari Grad SJB was the night after the killing of the member of the wedding party in Bascarsija. As I have told you, whenever grave crimes were committed, our colleagues from the Sarajevo SJB, or rather, from the Sarajevo CSB would engage us, would involve us in resolving these crimes together with them. They did so because the town SUP -- in our department, we also had the search and tracing department. So that same night, some two hours after the killing, together with several of police officers, whom I managed to reach because I think it was a Sunday, I started working on resolving this crime. Very quickly, we managed to find out who the perpetrators were, and we also received intelligence to the effect of where they were hiding. I think that from today's point of view -- I mean, looking at it now, I think our only mistake was that we informed about this the people who were above us, who were our superiors, and had already been deeply involved in some other business in addition to their regular police duties.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, just a minute, please. My specific question was: Did you go to see Mr. Bezdrob and Mr. Dahic that night, and what did you find upon going there? Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: When we got to the Stari Grad police station, it had been blocked by a taxi vehicle, so we were unable to approach it. We asked why the police station had been blocked, and two or three minutes later, the vehicles dispersed. When we went into the office of these gentlemen, it was the first time that I saw a radio -- a radio station that didn't belong to members of the Ministry of the Interior, and there was intense communication on this radio between members of the Patriotic League and the Green Berets. We realised that they were the ones who were practically co-ordinating all these activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you say it was a radio station, what sort of radio station was used by the MUP of the Socialist Republic of BH, and what was the radio station that you saw in that evening in the office of Enes Bezdrob and Ismet Dahic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The MUP of Republika Srpska had Motorolas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the MUP of Republika Srpska. I asked you about the MUP of the Socialist Republic of B&H.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I apologise, it was a slip of the tongue. The MUP of the Socialist Republic of B&H had standard Motorolas and this was an Alinco-make radio station. I remember that because sometime after that I, myself, had such a radio station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "after that," was that during your employment in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, or after that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: After that when I was employed in the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember when the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina split up?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The MUP split up sometime in early April of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who informed you that the MUP had been divided?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, I believe that it was my direct superior, Goran Macar, who informed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What instructions did you receive from your immediate superior, Goran Macar?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: We were told to continue going to work at the Sarajevo town SUP, to continue working, and that we would later see -- it would later turn out what this split would eventually look like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I was waiting for your explanation to something that you said a while ago in response to a question put to you by Counsel Zecevic. Namely, that you thought that the only mistake that you had made was to report the events after the killing in Bascarsija to your superiors. Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Could you explain what you mean by this? Why was it a mistake to report this to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that time in the CSB, the department chiefs in the CSB were my superiors at the time. Had we, the operatives who found out where these people were, gone and arrested them, some things might have evolved differently in Sarajevo. However, when I got to the Stari Grad police station, from the CSB to the police station, I could see that all the streets had been blocked. I went into the police station and then I realised - this was a multi-ethnic group that I was with -- I realised that we would never get to these perpetrators and that all the waiting that we had to endure before we actually went into action was just in order to hide the perpetrators. I know I was right then because I saw a television programme and I saw it Ramiz Delalic, Celo, who talked about this in 1993, and he bragged about the fact that it was the police who let him and his co-perpetrators out of Sarajevo. Unfortunately, already then, some of us were doing the police work professionally and some other people were engaged in other things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. May I remind you again to be as brief as you can in your responses. Just for clarification, do you mean to say that some of your superiors tipped off the perpetrators after you had informed them of what had happened and thus the perpetrators were able to disappear? Is that what you said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about this one specific case, and it's obvious that somebody in the chain of command failed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Back to you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, just a few questions. On page 24, you said, "At that time in the CSB, my superiors in the CSB," as far as I understood you at that time in 1992, in early 1992, you worked in the town SUP. So tell us, please, whether this was the town SUP or the CSB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: If we operatives from the town SUP assisted in discovering crimes, if we assisted operatives from the CSB and if they were hierarchically above us, then they were the ones who managed both me or my operatives and not somebody from the town SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that when you say that there was some problems with command and that information regarding the perpetrators leaked out, that this went along this line of hierarchy according to which you were involved in these tasks?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in early April where was your office located, in which building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In the building of the Sarajevo town SUP on the fourth floor. In August Cesarac Street, I don't know what the name of the street is today. This now houses the cantonal SUP of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: After your immediate superior Mr. Goran Macar informed you that MUP had been divided and that you were to continue working until the split is finalised structurally, did you continue with your work and your duties as you would normally?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, as long as that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: If you are moving on to something else, this would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have one question, Your Honour, then I would be moving to something else, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, which was the last day that you spent in that building of the town SUP?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe it was a Friday or a Saturday. I can't recall precisely, but it was in early April. 3rd -- the night between the 3rd -- the night between the 3rd and the 4th or the 4th and the 5th, I'm not really sure, but I know it was the end of the week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we take our first break for the day. We would resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, while the witness is ushered in, I'm afraid I'm not going to make things easier. When I was citing the pending motion, I forgot one, and that is our motion for adjudicated fact, which -- adjudicated facts, which is also, I think, important for us to have before the last witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. And we appreciate counsel's indulgence for the extended break but we communicated the reasons through our Legal Officer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We, while the witness is ushered in, ask OTP and the Zupljanin Defence about their estimates on the witness Macar, is that the name, Zecevic, your last one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Macar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Goran Macar. Can you assist us with that, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it's difficult with all these witnesses because what is on the 65 ter is never what comes out. Twenty hours is the estimate for the Defence. I would estimate probably not at much, but it's difficult to say how long, as I say, until we have a clear idea, particularly of documents that he is going to be taken through. But I'd say roughly in the region of between three and 4 days, so about 16 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Aleksic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ALEKSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, again, for the take sake of caution, I will say no more than three hours. We may not need any time at all, but just for the sake of caution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: May I continue, Your Honours? Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, before we continue discussing the details of what happened later, you mentioned that the chief of the sector at the town SUP was Mr. Goran Macar, how many operatives, how many inspectors were in that sector in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I am sorry, Goran Macar was the chief of the department, not the chief of the sector. Mr. Jozo Leotar was the chief of the sector. As for our department, I'll just need a minute to think about it. I think about eight inspectors.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition of these inspectors, was it mixed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the chief of the department, Mr. Goran Macar, informed you about the division of the MUP and, as you said, he instructed you to continue working as you had before, did Mr. Macar inform only you or all the employees in the department?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Everybody in the department knew that the MUP would be divided and we even joked about that. We joked about who would get which table and how we would cut up the tables. There was no bad feelings among us who were working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Another small digression before we get back to the events of April 1992, tell me, in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of B&H, technical equipment and materiel needed for the work of the MUP, was this equipment and materiel stored in a central location?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe that this was because I knew about one such warehouse. The police stations had only what they needed for their day-to-day work in the police stations themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Which warehouse did you know about, which central warehouse of the MUP did you know about?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: This is a warehouse that I never visited. It was somewhere towards Rakovica in a place called Duboki Potok or something like that, and that's where most of the equipment of the Republican MUP was located.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about a MUP facility called Zlatiste, and what do you know about it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I do know about the facility. I know where it was located, but I think it was a facility of the state security service, and we from public security station didn't have access to that a facility and to similar ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at document 140, that is 65 ter 757D1. Sir, the date of this document is the 3rd of July, 1991. It says the Ministry of the Interior, the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Sarajevo. It is addressed to the administration for financial matters and tasks. The subject is "order to relocate weapons and ammunition," and it is signed by Mesud Omerspahic. Tell me, did you know Mr. Omerspahic or have you heard of him, Mr. Mesud Omerspahic?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I did not know him personally except for the fact that through all this paperwork we knew that he was the head of office, the Chef de Cabinet, of Alija Delimustafic, the then minister of the interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, it is stated that upon an order of the minister MUP weapons and ammunition stored at the Rakovica facility has to be relocated forthwith to the Zlatiste facility, and protection and secrecy must be ensured in the implementation of this task. Did you know about that in 1991, that ammunition and weapons from the Rakovica facility was relocated to the Zlatiste facility?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the Rakovica facility, did it belong to the public security service or the state security?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, it belonged to the public security service. It was our property.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what about this facility Zlatiste, was that a facility with limited access?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it was a facility that was completely sealed off and, as I've already said, we had no access.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What service did it belong to, this facility?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The state security service.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember who was the chief of service of the state security service at that time in 1991?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I cannot recall exactly. I think it was Vesic or someone, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, for the sake of clarity, I would like to ask this document to be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On what basis? The witness says nothing about it. I am assuming he hasn't been asked, but he hasn't seen the document before. We don't know where the document comes from. I'm not at all clear on the basis on which it can be MFI'd.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner has asked the question I was just about to ask, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, perhaps the witness can take the -- his headphones off. Your Honours, the witness testified that he had knowledge of these two facilities. The provenance of the document is RS MUP, and we provided the Office of the Prosecutor with the list of all the documents we received from them. Now, the -- I agree that the witness does not know about the document and haven't seen it before, and he is not aware of the fact. But I would like to -- that is precisely why I ask that this document be MFI'd because the witness was talking about it -- was talking about these two facilities, and that's the main point which I'm trying to establish; namely, that on the order of the Ministry of the Interior, the ammunition and the arms have been moved from the official storage into secret other place owned by the state security and that this was a secret operation. And that is precisely why I think it's important for the context of the events that unfolded in the beginning of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry, but there's absolutely no evidence at all of this movement, nor the relevance to anything. And we say at the moment there's no basis at all for this document even being marked MFI.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, MFI pending what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, just because I've shown this document to the witness and he commented on it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: But what would allow us to lift, at any point, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I will show it to another witness who might be able to recognise the document, so just for the sake of the transcript that these two documents -- that the comments of this witness and, perhaps, another witness will be brought in connection. That is the only reason I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So pending the showing -- pending the testimony of --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Pending showing it to another witness or bar table motion, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: On the expectation, Mr. Zecevic, that you are able to show a nexus between this document and another witness, it will be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D573, marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, you told us that your last day was Friday or Saturday, sometime in the beginning of April. Tell me, at the time were you carrying out any preparations for transferring to the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, no. We were not carrying out any kind of preparations. I lived in Nedzarici. The population is mostly ethnic Serbs. And, as I said, I went home from work. I can support that with the following: All my personal belongings, my graduate records from university, all my other personal belongings, all of that remained in my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You said that you went home to Nedzarici. Tell me, where is Nedzarici, is that part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that is part of Sarajevo and it's between the airport of Sarajevo and Dobrinja and Alipasino Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which public security station does Nedzarici belong to from a territorial point of view, at that time that is?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: To the public security station of Novi Grad in Sarajevo, territorially speaking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell us what happened after you returned home from work on that Friday or Saturday.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: That evening, when I came home from work, attacks had already started against all police stations in Sarajevo. These attacks were being carried out by the Green Berets and the Patriotic League. I and a colleague of mine were assigned to tour those police stations that evening, and as I've already said, they were -- there were many members of the Green Berets and Patriotic League around at the time, for the time being -- I mean, at that time, they were still considered to be civilians, armed civilians, who surrounded the police stations. And very soon we found out that a policeman had been killed at the police station of Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, which policeman was killed?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Pero Petrovic was the policeman killed. He was a member of the police station for training dogs and horses. That police station was also under the SUP of Sarajevo, the town SUP of Sarajevo. According to what we knew then - and now I can speak about what I learned subsequently as well because in my work we did investigate that particular crime - this policeman caught a person who was breaking into the privately-owned vehicle of a neighbour of his who was a Bosniak, and they went together to hand that person over to the police station of Novo Sarajevo, because this policeman had lived in the territory of the municipality of Novo Sarajevo. And he acted in accordance with regulations. However, what happened was that once they arrived at that police station, a colleague of his who was the duty policeman stopped him and asked him to have a cup of coffee together with him. He stayed for that cup of coffee. However, at that moment, the Green Berets barged into that police station, or members of the Patriotic League. They took the shift leader prisoner and also this policeman who was wearing civilian clothes. They took him to the basement. And when they asked him what his name was, he said Pero Petrovic - otherwise, Pero Petrovic is a symbolic name for Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina - and one of these Green Berets simply shot him dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, on the next day, did you go to work? Did you manage to go to work?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No. That had already turned into mission impossible because the town of Sarajevo was blockaded, there were roadblocks in the streets yet again, and, quite simply, I could not leave my neighbourhood anymore. I could not enter the territory that was under the control of the Green Berets and the Patriotic League.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please have a look at document P986, which is tab 148. I don't know if you have it, but it is going to show up on the screen. That is a map of the town of Sarajevo. I'm sure that you are going to get a clearer picture on the screen. Sir, I don't know whether you will be able to but I would kindly ask you to mark the headquarters of the town SUP where your office was at the time. The usher will give you a pen. He will assist us kindly. And could you please put a circle around Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours, I didn't hear your suggestion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: My suggestion was to have the Registrar enlarge the map a bit, otherwise the witness will be unable to find the exact spot on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please wait, Mr. Tusevljak, we need to zoom in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The middle area of the map, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is this all right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no need for that. The previous one was fine. [In English] Can we have the map enlarged again, just once. Okay. That's enough. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, Mr. Tusevljak, would you please mark with an X the headquarters of the town MUP and put number 1 next to it.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I apologise, I first marked Nedzarici.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then put number 1 there. Now, would you please mark roughly where the town SUP was?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Put a 2 there.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now that we are dealing with this map, would you please show us -- or, rather, tell us, did you, and if so when, go to the school in Vrace after these events?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Since I found out that the headquarters of the Serbian Ministry of the Interior was in Vrace, I went perhaps on the 7th or 8th of April, 1992, to see what was happening and what was going on with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please mark with an X the school in Vrace and put a 3 there.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, what was the situation like when you arrived in the school at Vrace?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I need the witness to mark another location. So we can keep it like this until he marks another location and then we'll save it, or maybe we save it now and then ... okay. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak, tell me, please, when you arrived in Vrace, what did you find there? What was the situation like? What was the general situation like at that moment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: It was chaotic for the simple reason that on that occasion at the school I met only one operative whom I knew who worked at the SJB Novo Sarajevo, and who basically was lost himself. He didn't know what we needed to do. I think that in passing I also saw Mr. Dobro Planojevic, who at the time was the commander of the Centar police station, who had come with some of his policemen. I returned to Nedzarici and reported to the reserve police station, which was located in that neighbourhood, and I put myself at their disposal there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was there a conflict on at the time in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, there had already been clashes, both in Vrace and elsewhere in town. There were clashes between the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska and the Territorial Defence of the then Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, when did you return to Vrace again, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Some two or three days later, perhaps. I came again because it was still possible to pass by the Sarajevo airport, so I could reach the area, but I also wanted to see what needed to be done, where would I work, what would I do, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark on this document the airport and put an X and number 4 there.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What happened upon your second return it to Vrace? Were you given an assignment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, somebody from the then leadership told me to stay in Nedzarici. I think that I also received an appointment letter or something to that effect appointing me head of police in Nedzarici. That police station in Nedzarici never had the crime police before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you do then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In the following month, or perhaps a bit after that, I stayed in Nedzarici. I would occasionally come to Vrace whenever it was possible to pass through the Sarajevo airport. The Ministry of the Interior of Republika Srpska was already being established. Dobro Planojevic became chief of the crime police administration, and I was again given the role of a co-ordinator for the town of Sarajevo within the crime police. However, that role mostly involved me trying to find out where the operatives who had already left the town of Sarajevo were. Many of them were blocked, basically, blocked somewhere in town. And in the territory of Republika Srpska, there were mostly operatives who had their houses there and we also had available to us those who had managed to flee to Pale and to some other areas that were under the control of Republika Srpska. We started drawing up lists of those people --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. MR. ZECEVIC [Interpretation] Unless there are objections, I would tender this document marked by the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D574, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me show you tab 149 which is 65 ter 7D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 65 ter 7D1. 0007D1. If we can get the Serbian version as well, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, this document is dated 15th of May, 1992. It says the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior, Sarajevo. And it's entitled "List of the Operatives in the Territory of Sarajevo." And underneath that we see Tusevljak, Simo, co-ordinator for the town of Sarajevo. Can you please explain to us what this document means, what it is about, and what does it mean that you were the co-ordinator for the town of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: That's precisely what I told you. My task was to locate these operatives who had left the town. And based on the location where we found them, we were coming up with tasks and duties for them in that area. That was one task that needed to be done. The other thing was that these people had literally fled the town in their slippers. I had to inform Dobro Planojevic about how many operatives had left the territory of Sarajevo and were now in the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What kind of operatives are we talking about here?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: These are the operatives of the crime police who used to work in the territory of Sarajevo. They worked on general crime, white-collar crime cases, forensics, and counter-sabotage protection. You can also see here that out of ten police stations that used to exist in town, we have only five represented on this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does this list pertain to all operatives of the crime police whose whereabouts you knew -- rather, you knew that they had left the town of Sarajevo and these were the people that you could count on to become the members of the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, this list was drawn up based on the locations from which these operatives reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: To clarify this - did I understand you well - these are the persons who left the town of Sarajevo, they reported to some SJBs, and then these SJBs, in turn, informed you that these persons had reported that they had left Sarajevo. Did I understand you well?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, but at the time the phones were not working so we, as operatives, communicated among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you have to be -- you have to make a break between my question and your answer because a large portion of your answer was not recorded. This is why I had to go back and ask you again.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, obviously Mr. Zecevic heard me say, Where did he say that? Because it wasn't apparent. But I really think the proper way of dealing with this is if a part of the answer is being -- not Mr. Zecevic to clarify, but to do as he has normally done, which is to ask him to repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I wasn't aware that it wasn't recorded. Ms. Korner, only when you made a comment it became apparent to me that it wasn't recorded. Because I tried to stop the witness before giving an answer so he doesn't -- so he doesn't speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, could you please explain to us what this list is about again, please?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: This is the list of operatives who used to work in the territory of Sarajevo who had left the area which was under the control of the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska and then reported to some police stations or reserve police stations and placed themselves at their disposal; that is to say, they wanted to become members of the MUP of Republika Srpska. Among these persons, there were also people with whom I spoke on the phone, explaining to them that they could sign up to be placed at the disposal of the MUP of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since there are no objections, I would like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: What is the relevance, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The relevance, is, Your Honours, the number of policemen available at that point in the MUP of Republika Srpska. The criminal police inspectors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: But it doesn't really say that, does it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, we don't object. We don't agree that's a proper reading, and I'm going to re-examine -- re-examine, cross-examine on it. So we don't object to it being marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: As far as I have understood the witness, this list shows the names of some of the policemen who fled the city of Sarajevo after the attacks, and so the witness tried to get hold of them again, and so what?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well perhaps the witness can take his phones off again so I will explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you take off your headphones. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the point is the following: The witness came to Vrace. He was given a task to be a co-ordinator for the city of Sarajevo concerning the criminal police. Now, he is trying to gather all operatives from the criminal police available at the moment, which is mid-May, and that is the list of all the people who were operatives of the criminal police which were available to the MUP of Republika Srpska in Sarajevo at that point. I think that's very relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 1D575, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, apart from the people listed on this document, were there other operatives from the crime police who were available to you for work in the RS MUP in the territory of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No. This is the list that we made at the time for the town of Sarajevo. There were many more operatives in the town of Sarajevo who were unable to leave the town or who didn't report to the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, how long were you a co-ordinator for the town of Sarajevo, for the crime police?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe until I became chief of the crime police department of the then Romanija-Birac Security Services Centre because the town SUP no longer existed in the RS MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when you say Romanija-Birac CSB, are you referring to the CSB that was sometimes also called the Sarajevo CSB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, when the Serbian autonomous regions were created, the Romanija-Birac centre was sometimes called the Sarajevo centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when were you appointed, if you remember, chief of the crime police department in the Sarajevo CSB, Romanija-Birac, that is?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe that was in June. I don't have that letter of appointment so I can't be precise.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was anybody in that function before you, and if so, who was it?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe that Nikola Milanovic was in that function for a while but I don't know whether he had an actual letter of appointment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And where was the seat of the Romanija-Birac Sarajevo CSB at the time?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Initially, it was housed in the school in Vrace for a very short time, and then later on, sometime in July, it was Energoinvest in Lukavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is that the building --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown 1D574 again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's tab 148. And the original document is 5986, but could we get 574, that's the map that the witness marked. He marked certain locations in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you mark for us on this map, with a cross and the number 5, the building of Energoinvest in Lukavica where the CSB was located from July of 1992, please?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not sure whether we can record this exhibit under the same number or under an additional number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it has the same number. I understand technically there's no difficulty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I see the time, Your Honours, I don't know whether we are taking the break now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... If this is a convenient point, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: While the witness is on his way back in, returning to a matter that was raised at the beginning of today's sitting, and that is the Stanisic motion to add 41 documents to the 65 ter list. Bearing in mind the distinction between the addition of documents to the 65 ter list and their admission, we would wish the Prosecution to respond to the question of addition by tomorrow afternoon, and, of course, admission would fall to be decided as and when the applications arise.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I appreciate that, but I would say that it's somewhat unequal in arms. If Your Honour will recall the number of times we had to apply formally to add documents to our 65 ter list, and were given -- and the Defence was given the time to respond. There are 41 documents. As far as I can tell, most of the documents on the recent one are to do with this -- or their attempt is to get them in with this witness, as I said, we'll see where we are at the end of the day. I would respectfully ask that that matter be left until such time as we've seen where we go with this witness. I mean, tomorrow afternoon when it was filed yesterday afternoon is, with the greatest of respect, we would suggest, slightly unfair.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We are losing sight of the fact that the admission of these documents would still have to be decided. It's the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but they haven't even got -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It's the preliminary, if I may call it that, question of their being added to the 65 ter list at this stage, and it is only that first step that we are asking for this expedited response.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, but, Your Honour, the fact is they have gone half, 50 per cent, of the way through to getting them in by getting them on the 65 ter list. Most of these documents, I must say really fairly quickly, have been available to the Defence forever and ever. They say they've only just dug them out of EDS recently, which I am not going to go into at the moment. But we say it's unfair to only give us only effectively 48 hours to respond when we are entitled to 14 days and - just a moment, please, Mr. Zecevic - some of them are not even translated, so we have no idea what is in them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, the documents which we offered by the motion are not the documents we found on the EDS exclusively. There is -- if Your Honours will remember, there has been 130 documents which have been disclosed to us for the very first time signed by our client by the Office of the Prosecutor, and some of them are in the -- this motion. Therefore, it is not entirely our fault. And first and foremost, we have heard a number of times that Office of the Prosecutor was saying that there has been problems with the search engines. Well, as they have problems with the search engines, so do we. And this is the EDS and there's nothing we can do about it. Once the document will appear; on the other occasion, they will not appear. That is just beyond either of the parties. That's one thing. The second thing: Your Honour will remember that at least on 15 occasions during the Prosecutor's case, there has been a request for the expedited response by the Trial Chamber, and in all of these -- on each and every one of these occasions we accepted and gave our expedited response because we understood the reasons why it was requested from us. Therefore, I think there has been no inequality of arms in this case. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not saying we want the 14 days. I'm simply saying that tomorrow afternoon is just too short a period for us to -- and particularly, as I say, as we don't have translations for some of these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course, the ones that are not translated, that's then a wholly different category, and we take your point there.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
