utterances.text: I'm told - Mr. Smith is going to give me information - of the 41 documents, 19 have no translations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So could we expect your response in respect of the 41 minus 19?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, can I -- at the moment, obviously, I'm here. And can I come back to you tomorrow if we have a problem? Otherwise we'll obviously see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We would be grateful for your co-operation, Ms. Korner. Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If I may be of assistance, Your Honours, we are notified by VWS that 14 of these documents will be -- CLSS, I'm sorry. CLSS. That 14 of these documents have been translated and will be uploaded in the morning. So that means that only five are still pending translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic, as you continue, I would need five minutes before we rise for the day, so if the witness can be excused at that point because there's a ruling which has to be given in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honours. May I continue now, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I've been informed by the Registrar that you will have to mark the seat of the CSB Romanija-Birac Sarajevo with the X and the number 5 once again on the map because last time it wasn't recorded due to electronic problems. So if you could do that again.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Registrar to save this document under the number that we already had, 1D574.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, when talking about the general crime department, could you explain to us what this department contains in accordance with the regulations, as a structure?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: When talking about the general crime department only, it contains operative groups that investigate crimes in the field of classical crimes, as it were. That means there can be a department for property-related crimes, for sexual crimes, and a department for other types of crimes such as organised crime, drugs. That is mainly what the general crime department deals with.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Page 48, line 9, says sexual crimes. Sexual crimes. I believe you said something else?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: For murders and sexual crimes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Sexual and violent crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As for the sector of the crime prevention administration, what is in its purview? What was in its purview according to the law and the valid regulations at the time, that is in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Apart from the general crime department, there's also white-collar crime department, forensics department, fire prevention department, and counter-terrorism and counter-sabotage department. These are the five basic departments. However, the administration at the level of the ministry also had an operative department.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us explain that. At the level of the Security Services Centre, the sector for crime prevention, the crime prevention sector, if I calculate it correctly, it contained five different departments; is that correct? Did I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it should contain five different departments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at the level of the administration or the ministry, there is an additional sixth department, and its called the operative department?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe this was the case because the MUP of Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Interpreter didn't catch the end of the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HARHOFF
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't get the last part of the witness's answer. Could you ask him to repeat.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please repeat the end of your last answer.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At the Ministry of Bosnia and Herzegovina, there was also a chief of the operatives, so there was a department -- an operative department as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since we've seen that the sector of the crime prevention administration at the level of the CSB and the MUP, and I'm talking about the MUP of the Socialist Republic of B&H, what was the situation like at the level of the SJB in the crime prevention sector?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At the SJBs there were crime departments but there were no forensics departments. They dealt with general crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So did I understand you correctly, can you confirm, at the level of the SJB in the crime prevention sector there was only one department and that was the general crime department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the level of the Security Services Centre in the crime prevention administration there are five departments: The general crime department, the white-collar crime department, the forensics department, the fire prevention department, and the counter-terrorism and counter-sabotage department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at the level of the MUP, the MUP at the seat in the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, apart from these five, there was an additional sixth department which was the operative department; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Sir, when in July you were appointed chief of the crime prevention administration at the Sarajevo CSB, that is Romanija-Birac CSB in the Republika Srpska MUP, was the structure or the internal organisation of that sector identical to the organisation that existed in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, it was a mirror image of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that at the level of the Security Services Centre Sarajevo Romanija-Birac in the crime prevention sector you had these five departments that had existed previously in CSBs in the MUP of the Socialist Republic of B&H?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: We had them at the planning level but none of them existed in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What is the reason for that?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: We didn't have operatives. We didn't have people who had the expert knowledge in order to be able to do these jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you were chief of the crime prevention sector administration at the level of the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac in the RS MUP, what was the total number of inspectors that you had in that sector, the total number of inspectors that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Those to whom I was immediate supervisor, well, there were only three of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us their names, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I think Zeljko Rakic was among them, Sasa Blagojevic and a man called Pekic, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'll show you 1D331. That's tab 14. Could you take a look at that document. It's in your binder, it's tab number 14. It says here "crime prevention department" and then there are four names including yours. Are these the people who you talked about a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, this is a payroll list.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, in the crime prevention administration at the Sarajevo Romanija-Birac CSB, did you have a forensics department?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At the time I believe we had one forensics technician who had not done that work for a long time, Seko Niksic [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So you had only one man, but what period was that? You said at that time we had one, what period are you referring to, if you can remember?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I believe this was June.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tusevljak, what about material required for forensics?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At that point in time, that is to say in May and June, we had nothing. We tried to make due with what we had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, I understand that you are a professional policeman, but you have to understand that some of us here do not know what this would be, what you can make due with in terms of forensics. Can you be more specific and tell us what you did have and what you did not have and in which period of time and until when?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In fact, there was a lack of all the material required for forensics at the time. There was only a photo camera that the technician had, and that was absolutely insufficient. In addition to that camera, we did not have even film, and we didn't even have a lab where we could develop any film.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And how long did that situation go on in the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: All the way until the end of the summer of 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did the situation get any better then?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The situation did get somewhat better but not significantly so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, during your interview with the Prosecution last month, I believe, you drew a map, and I would like to show it to you so that you can give us your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is tab 209 and the document is 962D1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: While we are waiting for the document, Mr. Tusevljak, tell me, please, if you can remember how many public security stations were subordinated to the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac after it was established within the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: There were 22 public security stations and police stations, as far as I can remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember this map? The one that you see in front of you now?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, the colours that we see on the map, red and green, are these your inscriptions?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what does this denote? What is marked in red on this map? Pink.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: That's the territory that was under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, rather the then Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about these lines? The ones that are marked in pink or red?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: These are the lines of separation between the Territorial Defence of Republika Srpska and the Territorial Defence of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which remained more or less the same all the way up until the end of the war in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In order to make things clear for us, I would like to ask you to mark on this map some toponyms, if I can put it that way. Can you use the letter A to mark Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Nedzarici is in this small circle here in the middle.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please place the letter A there.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, maybe it's better if we have the bigger -- or rather, this map but enlarged once. Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please mark the airport with the letter B.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The letter C for the centre of the security services.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, letter D for Ilidza. Could you mark that, please.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now the letter E, please. Could you mark Vogosca with the letter E for me.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the airport that you marked with the letter B on this map, under whose control was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At the very beginning of the war, it was handed over to the international force UNPROFOR, and it was under the control of international forces throughout the war. Both sides of the airport were under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, as you can see here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You from the CSB, or rather, from the place where the CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac was, did you have any physical contact with Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, no, there was an interruption because the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina held about 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Likewise. It was not possible to reach it along the shortest route because --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Please answer my question. Did you have any physical contact with Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have any physical contact? I mean, when I say physical contact, I mean direct physical contact with Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How far away is Ilidza, approximately, under normal conditions from the place where the CSB was at that moment?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Six to 7 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What about Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: About 15 to 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, when you would leave the CSB in order to go to Vogosca or Ilidza, how long did you have to travel? How long was the route that you had to take?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: About 150 or 160 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you draw the route for us on this map, the route that you took to Vogosca and Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I can do it approximately.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Those roads are not even marked on this map. That would be it roughly, the route that led to Ilidza.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, why did you have to go all the way around in order to get to Ilidza and Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: These other roads that were closer were either under the control of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or others were constantly under sniper or artillery fire from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If there are no objections, I would like to tender this document, this map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D576, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The -- this document, I'm advised, is on -- a part of the motion yesterday, so it's marked for identification at this stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I can say about this one we don't object. He did -- he drew this in the interview which we had with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So it's admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, it is not yet on your list of documents, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I have a list of 205 tabs, and this is 209; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's correct, yes. But I thought that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We can handle that, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tusevljak -- I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, Your Honours, I was advised that we provided the updated list of documents yesterday or early today -- last night, yes. And it has all 209 tabs. I will instruct that it be again forwarded to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: We'll find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, did you have any communication with Ilidza, Vogosca, and Nedzarici?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, [Previous translation continued] ... because it's not clear from the earlier transcript. If by "you," Mr. Zecevic really means the witness personally, or that -- the MUP at the CSB because it isn't clear from the earlier answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat the question for you. The CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac, did it have any communication with the public security station of Ilidza?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, there was that communication that I drew for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the only communication -- if I understand what you are saying, the only communication you had was if someone from the CSB traverses 160 kilometres in order to get to Ilidza, or someone from Ilidza takes the same road in order to get to the CSB. Did I understand you properly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What was the situation with Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The same, perhaps it was about 30 odd kilometres closer though.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ilijas?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Absolutely the same. It's in the same area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. Tusevljak, during 1992 what was CSB Sarajevo Romanija-Birac surrounded by? I mean the building where the CSB was.

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Throughout 1992, and for as long as it was in Lukavica, it was under incessant artillery fire of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or the Territorial Defence, or it was shelled.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was your office in that building?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. It wasn't a proper police office. It used to be the cafeteria or something, so it wasn't a proper police office.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You did -- or, rather, did you work from that office?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, that was the only office I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We heard your earlier testimony to the effect that your home was in Nedzarici, the apartment where you lived. And, also, a moment ago, you told us that there was no communication between the CSB building and Nedzarici. Tell me, where did you live, sleep, et cetera, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: In the office where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did any other senior personnel from the CSB live in a similar way, if I can put it that way?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, all senior personnel were refugees except for the chief of the centre. We all slept in our offices.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Here it says "except for the chief of the centre," where did he sleep?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: He slept with us in the office, too. But the man was from Sokolac, so he could go to his home every now and then; whereas the rest of us could not go home at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, 1D106, that is tab number 1 in your binder. That is the document I'd like to show you now. Just a question before we move on to this document. Sir, in the beginning of your testimony today you were saying that public security stations dealt with less serious crime, if I can put it that way, whereas CSBs dealt with more serious crimes. I am talking about the MUP of the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Did the same principle apply in the MUP of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: As the CSB and specifically the crime prevention department, were you involved in operative work in the territory of the CSB, at least during this first period of time up until the end of the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Well, if you saw that payroll, who could be involved in operative work? There was no operative work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, according to the job description schematic, how many workers of the crime prevention department at the CSB of Sarajevo Birac Romanija should there have been?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I think that they envisaged about 100 workers, 100 members in these five departments who were well qualified. That many were supposed to work at the CSB.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When you say "workers," you are referring to inspectors mainly; right?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me repeat. When you say "workers," who do you have in mind? What profile of employees do you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I'm referring to inspectors who would be in charge of crime prevention dealing with regular general crime, with white-collar crime, fire prevention department, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How many inspectors did you have?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: The profile of inspectors changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell us about the period up until the end of the summer of 1992, how many inspectors did you have?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Four to five, sometimes three depending on the period of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And later?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At the end of 1992, when the Ministry of the Interior announced job vacancies, the number increased.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let us go back to the document before us. Sir, this is a report dated the 12th of July, 1992, signed by Milenko Karisik and Ljubinko Mitrovic on page 3. Do you know these two men?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes. Ljubinko Mitrovic was an operative at the centre, and Karisik, Milenko, I think, was an operative in Novo Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This report pertains to early July when the chief of the CSB sent these two men to Vogosca. It says here that their task was to review the crime situation in the Serbian municipality of Vogosca. Tell me, please, did you know about this report at the time in 1992?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I did. These operatives were sent by the chief of the centre, and I think that it was at the insistence of somebody from political circles, or perhaps from the government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, before this period of time and before this report, did you know what the situation was regarding crime in the Serbian municipality of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: No, not until this date. Nobody from the CSB went to Vogosca, nor did we receive any official dispatch from that police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Before this report, did you know that in Vogosca SJB they did not have the crime police at all?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I did not know about crime police existing there at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Was an instruction issued to the Vogosca SJB regarding that, and if so, what kind of an instruction? Was something of the sort done when they inspected this place?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Based on this official report of these operatives, one can see that they only spoke to the chief and to the assistant. It can also be seen here that the offices of the crime police were locked. The Vogosca public security station before the war had its own crime police department, and it was clear that none of the pre-war workers worked at the police station on the 9th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Following this report, was the crime police department founded in the Vogosca SJB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: It was agreed to set up the crime police but it wasn't done immediately because the operatives from the centre who had gone down there encountered problems, both with the chief of the station and with some other individuals.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, on page 2 of this document, the penultimate paragraph, last sentence of that paragraph reads: "Upon arrival of the Assistant Minister Dobro Planojevic to Vogosca, we spoke to him and told him about our observations regarding the situation, and we agreed that the crime service should be set up and that it should be made up of the following persons: Brane Vlaco, head of the service, current employee of the service and the Sarajevo CSB; Stanko Blagovcanin, and then" -- I apologise, I was rushing. So the following people would make up that service: Brane Vlaco, as the head of the service, hereto employee of the service and the Sarajevo CSB; the next person, Stanko Blagovcanin, employee of the Vogosca SJB dealing with crime; and then additional two persons. Tell me, please, this name, Vlaco, Brane, do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Who is it and what do you know about this person?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Brane Vlaco was an employee of the white-collar crime of the Sarajevo CSB. He may have been in some kind of a management position. He was there when the war broke out because he was originally from Vogosca. He signed up to work in this police station. So he was an inspector in our centre before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, I know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Did he have some kind of a specific feature? Did he have mustache, beard?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: At the time, he had mustache, I think. To this day that's true, but I haven't seen him for a number of years.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What happened after this, did Brane Vlaco become the chief of the crime prevention service at the Vogosca SJB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I don't think he did, and if he did by any chance, then he held that position for a very short period of time because soon thereafter he left the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know where he went and what he did?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I think that for awhile he was an inspector at the crime police administration in Bijeljina in the RS MUP, and then after that, he moved to some other positions that were not within the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know what he does today?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: I think he is a banker nowadays. I am not sure. I think that he is in the banking industry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Following this report, Mr. Tusevljak, was there another visit made to the Vogosca SJB?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Yes, following the problems that the operatives encountered there, I, too, was sent by the chief of the centre to Vogosca.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that was, roughly?

utterances.speaker: SIMO TUSEVLJAK
utterances.text: Also in July.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could we look at tab 2, 1D182.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, you haven't forgotten the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did, Your Honours. I apologise. Perhaps this is a good place to stop for the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Tusevljak, we are about to take the first adjournment for the day in the course of your testimony, and I remind you that having been sworn as a witness, you cannot have any communication with counsel from either side. Moreover, in such conversations as you have with anybody else, you cannot discuss your testimony. So we will continue tomorrow morning. The Court is not going to rise immediately, as we have other matters with which to deal. The usher will escort you from the courtroom, and we'll reconvene in this courtroom tomorrow morning. Thank you. Sorry, tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Could we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we rise to resume tomorrow at 2.30. I assume that counsel would have seen the -- today's change to the calendar where on Friday we are sitting in the -- sorry, 2.15 tomorrow. And I assume the counsel has seen the change whereby on Friday we are sitting in the morning, not in the afternoon. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 16th day of June, 2011, at 2.15 p.m. 20 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.59 p.m.
